Claude Fable 5 will be available again globally tomorrow.

After a series of productive conversations with the US government, we're redeploying the model with a new set of classifiers to target and block more cybersecurity tasks. In the near term, some routine tasks like coding and debugging will fall back to Opus 4.8. We’ll continue to refine these classifiers over the coming weeks to reduce false positives and better distinguish genuine misuse from legitimate requests.

We’ve also begun drafting a consensus framework—with Amazon, Microsoft, Google, and other Glasswing partners—for assessing the severity of AI jailbreaks and how AI developers should respond to them. We invite other industry partners and model providers to join us in this effort.

Finally, we’re scaling up our collaboration with the US government on model testing and safeguards. This will include pre-release access to models and safeguards for evaluation, information sharing on jailbreaks and misuse, and dedicated resources for joint research.

Thank you to our users for your patience, and to our partners across the government, industry, and the research community who worked alongside us to make Fable 5 available again.

data.text:
【7月1日 夜のニュースまとめ】
・Claude Fable 5の輸出規制が解除され復活
・Sonnet 5、実質コスト高もビジネスタスクで高評価
・ソフトバンクGがOpenAIへ100億ドル追加出資
・経産省が国産AI新会社に3873億円支援
・GPT-5.6 SolがGeneBench-Proで高評価
・MCPサーバー実装の5つの頻出パターン分類記事が公開
・LLM-as-a-Judgeの効果的な評価手法BINEVAL
・Hugging Faceに80TBの天体物理学データセット公開
・Kaggleチュートリアル第7版が公開

===

Claude Fable 5の輸出規制が解除され復活【続報】

・米国政府によるAnthropicのモデル利用制限に関する続報です
・米国商務省がClaude Fable 5およびMythos 5の輸出規制を解除し、グローバルでの利用が再開されました
・7月7日までは週次利用上限の50%までサブスクリプション内で利用可能ですが、それ以降は従量課金に移行します
・サイバーセキュリティタスクをブロックする新たな分類器が導入され、一部のコーディングタスクはOpus 4.8にフォールバックする仕様となっています

===

Sonnet 5、実質コスト高もビジネスタスクで高評価【続報】

・Claude Sonnet 5に関する続報です。
・トークン単価は安いものの、タスク完了により多くのトークンを消費するため、実質的なコストがOpus 4.8よりも高くなるとの指摘が相次いでいます。
・一方で、スプレッドシート操作や資料作成などの高度なビジネスタスクにおいては、Opusを上回る性能を示していると評価されています。
・旧モデルから引き継がれた日本語の自然さや、エージェントとしての素直さも高く評価されており、用途に応じた使い分けが推奨されています。

===

ソフトバンクGがOpenAIへ100億ドル追加出資【続報】

・ソフトバンクグループによるOpenAIへの投資に関する続報です。
・同社がOpenAIに対して新たに100億ドル（約1兆6000億円）の追加出資を行ったことが報じられました。
・桁違いの投資規模に多くの開発者や業界関係者から驚きの声が上がっており、AI分野における覇権争いのさらなる激化が予想されます。

===

経産省が国産AI新会社に3873億円支援【続報】

・以前報じられた官民連携による国産AI開発の新会社設立に関する続報です。
・経済産業省がこの新会社に対して、3873億円の大規模な支援を行うことが明らかになりました。
・国内のAI開発力を強化し、グローバルな競争力を高めるための重要な一歩として注目を集めています。

===

GPT-5.6 SolがGeneBench-Proで高評価【続報】

・OpenAIの計算生物学向けベンチマーク「GeneBench-Pro」に関する続報です
・GPT-5.6 Solが同ベンチマークで大きな進歩を示したとGreg Brockman氏が報告しました
・人間の専門家が20〜40時間かかる複雑な分析タスクをこなせるかが焦点となっており、科学研究におけるAIエージェントの実用化が着実に進んでいます

===

MCPサーバー実装の5つの頻出パターン分類記事が公開

・MCPサーバーを構築する際に頻出する5つの実装パターンを分類した記事が共有されました。
・独立して開発された15のサーバーを分析し、共通するアーキテクチャのパターンを体系化しています。
・AI開発チームが同じ構造を車輪の再発明してしまうのを防ぐための有用なタクソノミーとして、開発者に一読が推奨されています。

===

LLM-as-a-Judgeの効果的な評価手法BINEVAL

・LLMを評価者として用いる「LLM-as-a-Judge」において、より効果的な評価を行うための手法「BINEVAL」の論文が紹介されました。
・全体的なスコア付けでは推論過程や天井効果が隠れてしまう問題を解決するため、評価基準をアトミックな要素に分解して評価を行います。
・AIエージェントやモデルの出力をより正確かつ透明性高く評価する手法として関心を集めています。

===

Hugging Faceに80TBの天体物理学データセット公開

・Hugging Faceに30以上のソースから収集された80TBに及ぶ天体物理学のデータセットが公開されました。
・銀河の画像やスペクトルデータなどが含まれており、約4GBのRAM環境でもロード可能な設計になっています。
・AIと科学を掛け合わせた「AI x Science」分野における非常に大規模で重要なリリースとして注目されています。

===

Kaggleチュートリアル第7版が公開【続報】

・執筆が進められていた「Kaggleのチュートリアル」第7版が完成し、公開されました
・公開に合わせて無料キャンペーンの実施も発表されています
・最新のコンペティション動向やテクニックを学ぶための有用なリソースとして歓迎されています

I'm pretty sympathetic to where the administration and Anthropic landed on Fable, precisely *because* of the existence of a controlled access program intended to buy down risk across commercial IT products prior to the democratized deployment of advanced AI systems capable of cyber reasoning (i.e., Glasswing/Mythos).

Here's what I had previously written on the ideal systematic approach. The problems we've seen in this episode are that we don't necessarily have the clear benchmarks, independent standards, and technocratic bodies called for in this approach or at least we haven't synthesized them into a standardized collaborative process. It's a bit naïve to think that we'd have done so by now though -- technocratic diplomatic solutions often emerge only after a bit of warring and compellence. Such is the nature of the beast.

"The primary means to control foreign cyber actors’ access to advanced AI systems are the development and implementation of technical safeguards in advanced AI products. Frontier AI companies have already implemented these safeguards, which limit customers’ use of advanced AI systems for exploit development and cyber operations while permitting security engineering, code analysis, bug discovery, red teaming, enumeration of cybersecurity risks, and context-dependent research and education about persons, IT products, and networks. 

Cyber actors, however, can circumvent these safeguards through clever prompt engineering, posing as cybersecurity or security engineering specialists while in fact researching target technologies and networks for offensive purposes, or reverse engineering patching or security engineering work.

As AI models become increasingly performant in technical tasks associated with cyber operations, AI labs and independent researchers should invest more in the testing, development, and implementation of effective safeguards that more accurately distinguish between defensive and offensive research. 

Where independent testing and observation reveals the inefficacy of such safeguards above a predefined acceptable standard — or else reveals, according to an independent standard, that AI products’ limited code analysis, IT product research, or risk enumeration capabilities are sufficiently useful for offensive tasks such as offensive vulnerability research or mission planning — AI companies should implement more restrictive safeguards that limit use of their commercially available products for even benign information security tasks, research, and education.

Given that the vast majority of AI customers do not conduct information security-related work, this should not substantially affect lab monetization or the release schedules for their principal products. Such safeguards may, however, affect how effective advanced AI-driven coding agents or integrated development environments are in producing secure software. 

These tradeoffs are to some extent irreconcilable, but they can be softened through development and implementation of more effective techniques to discriminate between offensive and defensive vulnerability research, security engineering, and cybersecurity risk management. These techniques can be developed and tested by the AI labs themselves, third-party evaluation organizations, Center for AI Security and Innovation (CAISI), and NSA, all of whom would likely benefit from greater resources, compute budgets, and model access.

AI products without restrictive safeguards on information security-related work should be made available via controlled product releases to authorized users in the security engineering, cybersecurity, and red teaming roles within key industries. Particularly important are security engineering teams at major IT product companies whose firewalls, virtual private networking devices (VPNs), servers, operating systems, and applications are likely vulnerability research priorities for foreign offensive actors. 

These personnel should be provided access initially as part of focused vulnerability research activities such as those elaborated on below. AI products with substantial information security capabilities should be made increasingly available to broader communities of users, including cybersecurity companies for backend integration into their products and priority security operations centers, as risk is systematically attenuated.

This multi-prong gambit, it should be noted, presents a clear tradeoff, albeit one that is impossible to manage via a strategy developed a priori. By restricting access to cyber-capable models and therefore coding agents’ and integrated development environments’ ability to leverage these models, the United States would limit the extent to which the broader IT and developer community uses advanced AI systems to program secure software. Our overall resiliency strategy, however, relies on the use of these AI-powered systems to, by default, increase the security of software produced economy-wide, starting with the most vulnerable devices and software applications used across the IT economy.

To the extent that safeguards that limit advanced AI models’ use in security-related tasks and advanced cyber models are released in a controlled fashion, this will delay most developers’ and security engineers’ access to the most performant secure software generation technologies and therefore make their products less secure or more expensive to secure (while also limiting other defenders’ access to advanced AI capability). 

Because technologies used for offensive and defensive vulnerability research, code analysis and security engineering (especially where it involves iterated code reviews and security testing), and exploit and patch development are often indistinguishable, this tradeoff is tough to soften. One potential solution is through product safeguards that limit advanced vulnerability research and security engineering capabilities in coding agents or integrated development environments to codebases that are developed largely within such a system or else demonstrably one’s own.

Effective controlled product release will require AI labs to implement robust know-your-customer regimes. Intelligence services and military cyber actors maintain covered procurement mechanisms, e.g., personas with forged documents, coopted contractors, to circumvent such systems. Depending on the severity of the risks of foreign cyber actors’ acquiring access to these controlled systems, these know-your-customer regimes could be constructed around private identification data, authenticated corporate e-mail accounts, or AI lab-distributed hardware-based authentication mechanisms.

Advanced AI system release schedules should be informed by AI lab, CAISI, NSA, and third-party risk evaluations as to: 

(1) how effective unrestricted models are in conducting offensive cyber, including vulnerability research, tasks; 
(2) how effective relevant safeguards and know-your-customer mechanisms are in restricting malign use; and 
(3) how much national cybersecurity risk has been mitigated through product security and cybersecurity capability improvements. 

The ultimate objective of these evaluations is to determine when expanded capability release is likely to decrease cybersecurity risk rather than increase it. Detailed evaluations against well-designed performance benchmarks (e.g., those that determine an AI system’s efficacy in developing clandestine implants, defeating application or endpoint monitoring, accurately identifying target-specific persistence and exfiltration mechanisms) can help calibrate our understanding of these risks, thereby informing product release schedules better than the status quo heuristics of lab personnel."
